title: Banda's end
hookLine: Banda is tortured and killed in Delhi, with his young son

lines: A COT BY A RIVER AT NANDED.
cards: A cot by a river at Nanded. A hermit hurries home, finds a stranger sitting where no one sits, and ends the day calling himself that stranger's banda, his servant.
On this path that was only nine days ago; in the story, it's years.
The servant carried five arrows north, took towns, struck coins in his Gurus' names, gave fields to farmers, ran through the hills, starved behind mud walls, and was marched in chains to Delhi.
Now his companions are gone, and his own turn has come.

teach.h: BROUGHT OUT WITH HIS YOUNG SON.
teach.b: Sikh tellings of Banda Singh's last day are hard, and they don't need to be told in full to be understood. He was brought out in Delhi with his young son, Ajai Singh.
Tradition says he was offered his life, as the others were, if he would give up his faith, and he refused.
Then the hardest part of the telling: tradition says his little boy was killed in front of him, and that Banda Singh did not break. Then he himself was put to death, slowly, by torture.

teach.h: THE TELLINGS DWELL ON HIS STILLNESS.
teach.b: The tellings dwell less on the pain than on his stillness.
Some say an official asked him how a man who had done so much could come to this, and that he answered calmly, speaking of God's will and of how wrongdoers are punished in God's time.
The exact words vary, and it's best not to put new ones in his mouth. That's the line: he did not break.
Not that he wasn't hurt, or wasn't afraid. Only that what he'd chosen at that cot by the river stayed chosen to the end. Sikhs remember him by the fuller name, Banda Singh Bahadur, the brave.
They remember him in more than one way, too; parts of his story were argued over by Sikhs who came after, and that's a story for tomorrow. But on this day the memory is simple.
The man who began by calling himself a servant ended as one, keeping faith with the One he served.

how: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur's death in Delhi, with his young son Ajai Singh, as a martyrdom, and honor him by the name Bahadur, the brave.

games.q: you're Banda Singh, in chains in Delhi, and offered your life if you give up your faith. what do the tellings say he did?
o: refused, and stayed still to the end.
games.why: tradition says he refused, and that even when his son was killed before him, he did not break.

practice: If you have a candle, a lamp, or even a phone light, set it in front of you; if not, picture a small flame, and look at it without staring.

Let it stand for the people who didn't break: Banda Singh, his son, the captives in Delhi, and anyone you know of, in any time, who kept faith under pressure. You don't need words; if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Banda's end. The death of Banda Singh Bahadur in Delhi, with his young son, when, tradition says, he refused to give up his faith and did not break.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Banda Singh Bahadur, Banda Singh the brave.

carryVoice: Your line: he did not break. The servant's story ends in stillness. That's day eight hundred forty-six.
